propositions.text: Prairie Pride Natural Foods Ltd. filed an application for judicial review of a Canada Agricultural Review Tribunal decision.
propositions.quote: Prairie Pride Natural Foods Ltd. has filed an application for judicial review of a decision of the Canada Agricultural Review Tribunal (Tribunal) cited as 2022 CART 21 (Decision).

paragraphs.summary: Prairie Pride Natural Foods Ltd. filed an application for judicial review of a Canada Agricultural Review Tribunal decision, says the court.

propositions.text: Prairie Pride operates a poultry processing business in Saskatchewan and was served a violation notice on April 10, 2022.
propositions.quote: Prairie Pride operates a poultry processing business based in Saskatchewan. On April 10, 2022, the corporation was served with a notice of violation pursuant to s. 9(2)(c) of the Agriculture and Agri-Food Administrative Monetary Penalties Act, S.C. 1995, c. 40 (Act).

propositions.text: The notice alleged transporting chickens with defective tarps and inadequate ventilation, described as very serious, with a $15,000 penalty imposed.
propositions.quote: The notice alleges that the applicant transported chickens in a truck with defective tarps and inadequate ventilation. The violation was described as “very serious” and a penalty in the amount of $15,000 was imposed.

paragraphs.summary: Prairie Pride operates a poultry business and was served a violation notice alleging serious transport defects with a $15,000 penalty, says the court.

propositions.text: Prairie Pride requested a review by the Tribunal on May 9, 2022.
propositions.quote: On May 9, 2022, Prairie Pride requested a review of the violation by the Tribunal.

propositions.text: The Tribunal found the review request inadmissible for not being made in the prescribed time and manner.
propositions.quote: On July 8, 2022, the Tribunal determined that the request was inadmissible because it had not been made in the time and manner prescribed.

paragraphs.summary: Prairie Pride requested a review on May 9, 2022, but the Tribunal found it inadmissible for untimeliness, says the court.

propositions.text: Prairie Pride filed this judicial review application on August 8, 2022, seeking to quash or set aside the Tribunal's decision.
propositions.quote: On August 8, 2022, Prairie Pride filed this application for judicial review, which seeks to have the Decision quashed or set aside.

paragraphs.summary: Prairie Pride filed a judicial review application on August 8, 2022, seeking to quash the Tribunal's decision, says the court.

propositions.text: Prairie Pride argues the Tribunal erred in concluding the review request was improperly made.
propositions.quote: With respect to the merits, Prairie Pride submits that the Tribunal was wrong to conclude that the request for review was not properly made.

propositions.text: Prairie Pride alleges a procedural fairness breach as it was not given an opportunity to be heard.
propositions.quote: With respect to procedural fairness, Prairie Pride submits that its rights to procedural fairness were breached because the Tribunal did not provide it with an opportunity to be heard.

paragraphs.summary: Prairie Pride argues the Tribunal erred on the review request's validity and breached procedural fairness by denying a hearing opportunity.

propositions.text: The application is allowed based on the merits; procedural fairness need not be addressed.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I would allow the application based on the merits of the Decision. It is not necessary to discuss whether there has been a breach of procedural fairness.

propositions.text: Whether the Tribunal reasonably found the review request was not properly made is the issue.
propositions.quote: II. Did the Tribunal reasonably find that the request for review was not properly made?

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the application on merits and will not address procedural fairness; the issue is the Tribunal's reasonableness on the review request.

propositions.text: Prairie Pride sent the review request by email on May 9, 2022, and followed up by registered mail on May 18, 2022, received May 24, 2022.
propositions.quote: Prairie Pride sent the request for review to the Tribunal by email on May 9, 2022. This was followed up by sending a copy by registered mail on May 18, 2022. The copy was received on May 24, 2022.

paragraphs.summary: Prairie Pride emailed the review request May 9, 2022, then sent a registered mail copy May 18, received May 24, says the court.

propositions.text: The Tribunal found the review request was late because the copy was sent after the May 12, 2022 deadline.
propositions.quote: The Tribunal determined that the request for review was not made in the time prescribed because the copy was sent late. It was required to be sent by May 12, 2022 and it was actually sent on May 18, 2022.

paragraphs.summary: The Tribunal found the review request late because the copy was sent after the May 12 deadline, says the court.

propositions.text: Section 9(2)(c) of the Act allows a person served a violation notice to request a review in the prescribed time and manner.
propositions.quote: A person who is served with a notice of violation under the Act is entitled to request a review in the time and manner prescribed. The relevant provision is paragraph 9(2)(c) of the Act: 9(2) Instead of paying the penalty set out in a notice of violation or, where applicable, the lesser amount that may be paid in lieu of the penalty, the person named in the notice may, in the prescribed time and manner, 9(2) À défaut d’effectuer le paiement, le contrevenant peut, dans le délai et selon les modalités réglementaires: … … (c) request a review by the Tribunal of the facts of the violation. c) demander à la Commission de l’entendre sur les faits reprochés.

paragraphs.summary: The Act's s.9(2)(c) allows requesting a review in the prescribed time and manner, says the court.

propositions.text: Regulations specify the time and manner to request a review, including written requests within 30 days and delivery methods.
propositions.quote: The prescribed time and manner to request a review is set out in regulations promulgated by the Minister of Agriculture and Agri-Food pursuant to subsection 4(1) of the Act. The pertinent regulations are contained in subsections 11(2), 14(1) and 14(3) of the Agriculture and Agri-Food Administrative Monetary Penalties Regulations, S.O.R./2000-187, as amended (Regulations).

propositions.text: Request must be in writing within 30 days after notice served, by hand, registered mail, courier, fax or electronic means.
propositions.quote: 11(2) Where a person named in a notice of violation that contains a penalty requests, pursuant to subsection 9(2) of the Act, a review of the facts of the violation by the Minister or the Tribunal or, if the penalty is $2,000 or more, to enter into a compliance agreement with the Minister, the request shall be made in writing within 30 days after the day on which the notice is served. … 14(1) A person may make a request referred to in section 11, 12 or 13 by delivering it by hand or by sending it by registered mail, courier or fax or other electronic means to a person and place authorized by the Minister.

propositions.text: If sent by fax or electronic means, a copy must be sent by courier or registered mail within 48 hours after the time limit for making the request.
propositions.quote: 14(3) If a request is sent by fax or other electronic means, a copy of the request shall be sent either by courier or registered mail within 48 hours after the time limit for making the request.

paragraphs.summary: Regulations require written review requests within 30 days by specified methods; electronic requests require a copy by courier or registered mail within 48 hours after deadline.

propositions.text: The Tribunal must decide on review request admissibility within 60 days and notify parties in writing.
propositions.quote: The Rules of the Review Tribunal (Canada Agricultural Review Tribunal), S.O.R./2015-103 provide that the Tribunal is required make a decision on the admissibility of a request for review within 60 days and send the decision to the parties in writing. Rule 32(1) is set out below.

paragraphs.summary: The Tribunal must decide review request admissibility within 60 days and notify parties in writing, says the court.

propositions.text: The reasonableness standard requires the court to ensure the decision is transparent, intelligible and justified (Vavilov).
propositions.quote: In considering the Decision, the Court must apply the deferential standard of review of reasonableness (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65, [2019] 4 S.C.R. 653 at para. 17 (Vavilov)). This requires that the Court “consider the outcome … in light of [the] underlying rationale in order to ensure that the decision as a whole is transparent, intelligible and justified” (Vavilov at para. 15).

paragraphs.summary: The court must apply the reasonableness standard ensuring the decision is transparent, intelligible and justified, per Vavilov, says the court.

propositions.text: The issue is whether the Tribunal reasonably found the review request inadmissible due to the late follow-up copy.
propositions.quote: The issue, then, is whether the Tribunal reasonably found that the request for review was inadmissible because the follow-up copy of the request was out of time.

propositions.text: The Tribunal was correct that the copy was sent late, but it is questioned if sending the copy is necessary for a valid request.
propositions.quote: The Tribunal was correct that a copy of the request was sent late. However, a question remains: Is sending the copy necessary to have a valid request for review?

paragraphs.summary: The issue is whether the Tribunal reasonably found the request inadmissible due to late copy; sending the copy's necessity is questioned, says the court.

propositions.text: The Tribunal found the request invalid due to strict deadlines, relying on Clare and Hershkovitz decisions.
propositions.quote: The Tribunal determined that the request for review was invalid because the prescribed deadlines are strict (Decision at paras. 4, 15, 16). This conclusion was based on two decisions of this Court: Clare v. Canada (Attorney General), 2013 FCA 265, 451 N.R. 349 at para. 24 (Clare); and Hershkovitz v. Canada (Attorney General), 2021 FCA 38, 328 A.C.W.S. (3d) 431 (Hershkovitz).

paragraphs.summary: The Tribunal found the request invalid due to strict deadlines, relying on Clare and Hershkovitz, says the court.

propositions.text: The court has concerns relying on Clare and Hershkovitz as neither addresses the follow-up copy requirement.
propositions.quote: I have a concern with relying on these decisions because neither Hershkovitz nor Clare deals with the requirement to send a follow-up copy of a request for review.

paragraphs.summary: The court is concerned Clare and Hershkovitz do not address the follow-up copy requirement, says the court.

propositions.text: Hershkovitz concerns a different statutory requirement unrelated to the follow-up copy issue.
propositions.quote: The Hershkovitz decision concerns an entirely different statutory requirement, which has no similarity to the requirement at issue.

paragraphs.summary: Hershkovitz concerns a different statutory requirement unrelated to the follow-up copy, says the court.

propositions.text: Clare deals with the deadline for sending the original request and holds a late request is invalid.
propositions.quote: Clare deals with the deadline for sending the original request for review. This Court concluded in Clare that a request for review is invalid if it is not made within the time prescribed.

paragraphs.summary: Clare deals with the original request deadline and holds late requests invalid, says the court.

propositions.text: The statutory language for sending the original request differs materially from that for sending a follow-up copy.
propositions.quote: The relevant statutory language for sending the original request is materially different from the language for sending a follow-up copy.

propositions.text: The Tribunal did not discuss these differences or subsection 14(3) regarding the follow-up copy.
propositions.quote: These differences were not discussed by the Tribunal. Further, the Tribunal did not discuss the statutory language in subsection 14(3) at all.

propositions.text: The question is whether the Tribunal's decision is reasonable despite these omissions.
propositions.quote: The question is whether the Decision of the Tribunal is reasonable in spite of this.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the statutory language differs for original and follow-up requests; the Tribunal did not discuss this or s.14(3); reasonableness is questioned.

propositions.text: Vavilov paragraph 122 guides that minor omissions in statutory interpretation do not undermine decisions unless key elements are ignored causing unreasonableness.
propositions.quote: Vavilov provides useful guidance on the reasonableness standard of review in circumstances such as this, at paragraph 122: [122] It can happen that an administrative decision maker, in interpreting a statutory provision, fails entirely to consider a pertinent aspect of its text, context or purpose. Where such an omission is a minor aspect of the interpretive context, it is not likely to undermine the decision as a whole. It is well established that decision makers are not required “to explicitly address all possible shades of meaning” of a given provision: Construction Labour Relations v. Driver Iron Inc., 2012 SCC 65, [2012] 3 S.C.R. 405, at para. 3. Just like judges, administrative decision makers may find it unnecessary to dwell on each and every signal of statutory intent in their reasons. In many cases, it may be necessary to touch upon only the most salient aspects of the text, context or purpose. If, however, it is clear that the administrative decision maker may well, had it considered a key element of a statutory provision’s text, context or purpose, have arrived at a different result, its failure to consider that element would be indefensible, and unreasonable in the circumstances. Like other aspects of reasonableness review, omissions are not stand-alone grounds for judicial intervention: the key question is whether the omitted aspect of the analysis causes the reviewing court to lose confidence in the outcome reached by the decision maker. (Emphasis added)

paragraphs.summary: Vavilov para 122 guides that minor omissions in statutory interpretation do not undermine decisions unless key elements are ignored causing unreasonableness.

propositions.text: If a decision-maker omits a key statutory element and might have decided differently, the omission is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The emphasized passage from Vavilov above instructs that, if the Tribunal failed to consider a key element of the text, context or purpose of a statutory provision, and it is clear that the Tribunal may have arrived at a different conclusion if it had done so, the failure to do so is unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court states omitting a key statutory element that might change the decision is unreasonable, per Vavilov.

propositions.text: Tribunal did not consider text, context or purpose of subsection 14(3)
propositions.quote: Here, the Tribunal did not consider the text, context or purpose of subsection 14(3).

propositions.text: If Tribunal had considered these, it may have reached a different conclusion on admissibility
propositions.quote: if the Tribunal had done so, it is clear that it may have come to a different conclusion on the admissibility of the request.

propositions.text: Will discuss text, context and purpose of subsection 14(3) below
propositions.quote: Below I discuss the text and context of subsection 14(3), and then the purpose of the provision.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Tribunal failed to consider subsection 14(3)'s text, context, and purpose, which might have changed its admissibility decision.

propositions.text: Paragraph 9(2)(c) entitles a person to request Tribunal review in prescribed time and manner
propositions.quote: Paragraph 9(2)(c) of the Act provides that a person is entitled to request a review by the Tribunal “in the prescribed time and manner”.

propositions.text: Time and manner are set out in the Regulations
propositions.quote: The time and manner are set out in the Regulations.

propositions.text: Subsections 11(2) and 14(1) of Regulations provide prescribed time and manner to request review
propositions.quote: Subsections 11(2) and 14(1) of the Regulations explicitly provide a prescribed time and manner to make a request for review.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that paragraph 9(2)(c) and Regulations set the time and manner for requesting Tribunal review.

propositions.text: Subsection 11(2) sets time requirement: request must be made within 30 days after notice served
propositions.quote: It provides that “the request shall be made … within 30 days after the day on which the notice is served” (Emphasis added).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes subsection 11(2) requires requests within 30 days after notice service.

propositions.text: Manner of request is set out in subsections 11(2) and 14(1) of Regulations
propositions.quote: The manner of making the request is set out in subsections 11(2) and 14(1) of the Regulations.

propositions.text: Subsection 11(2) requires request to be made in writing
propositions.quote: Subsection 11(2) provides that the request must be “made in writing”.

propositions.text: Subsection 14(1) allows request delivery by hand, registered mail, courier, fax or electronic means
propositions.quote: Subsection 14(1) provides that a “person may make a request … by delivering it by hand or by sending it by registered mail, courier or fax or other electronic means …”.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the Regulations require requests in writing and allow various delivery methods including electronic means.

propositions.text: Subsection 14(3) does not explicitly link sending a copy with manner of making a valid request
propositions.quote: Unlike these Regulations, subsection 14(3) does not explicitly link the requirement to send a copy with the manner to make a valid request for review.

propositions.text: Subsection 14(3) requires sending a copy by courier or registered mail if request made electronically
propositions.quote: subsection 14(3) provides that if a request is made by electronic means, a copy of the request is required to be sent by courier or registered mail.

propositions.text: Sending the copy is mandatory but not stated as a requirement to make the request
propositions.quote: Although the text states that sending the copy is mandatory, it does not state that the copy is a requirement to make the request.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds subsection 14(3) mandates sending a copy if electronic but does not make it a requirement to make the request.

propositions.text: Tribunal's interpretation may be supported because subsections 14(3) and 14(1) are in same section
propositions.quote: One thing that might be said in favour of the Tribunal’s interpretation is that subsections 14(3) and 14(1) are both located in section 14.

propositions.text: Language in subsection 14(3) distinguishes manner of making request and requirement to send copy
propositions.quote: the language in subsection 14(3) itself distinguishes between the manner of making the request (electronic means) and the requirement to send a copy.

propositions.text: Language implies copy is not a requirement of making the request
propositions.quote: the language in subsection 14(3) seems to imply that the copy is not a requirement of making the request.

paragraphs.summary: The court acknowledges Tribunal's argument but finds subsection 14(3) language implies copy is not required to make the request.

propositions.text: Tribunal's interpretation causes inconsistency in deadlines for making request and sending copy
propositions.quote: it results in an inconsistency as to the deadline for making the request.

propositions.text: Deadline for making request is 30 days after notice service per subsection 11(2)
propositions.quote: subsection 11(2) provides a deadline for making the request of 30 days after the date of service of the notice of violation.

propositions.text: Deadline for sending copy is 48 hours after time limit for making request per subsection 14(3)
propositions.quote: The deadline for the copy is “48 hours after the time limit for making the request.”

propositions.text: Sending copy as requirement to make request creates internal inconsistency in deadlines
propositions.quote: Tribunal’s determination that sending a follow-up copy is a requirement to make the request produces an internal inconsistency in the deadline for making a request for review.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Tribunal's view creates inconsistent deadlines for request and copy, causing internal inconsistency.

propositions.text: Reviewed Regulatory Impact Analysis Statements (RIAS) on subsection 14(3) in current and earlier versions
propositions.quote: I have reviewed the Regulatory Impact Analysis Statements (RIAS) concerning the relevant provision, in its current and earlier versions.

propositions.text: Original subsection 14(3) had no fixed deadline and RIAS did not discuss its purpose
propositions.quote: The original version of subsection 14(3) had no fixed deadline and the RIAS did not discuss the purpose of the provision.

propositions.text: Subsection 14(3) amended in 2016 to provide fixed deadline; RIAS said amendments improved clarity and consistency
propositions.quote: Subsection 14(3) was amended in 2016 to provide for a fixed deadline. The relevant RIAS related to a number of amendments, including subsection 14(3), that were made to improve clarity and consistency of the Regulations.

propositions.text: Subsection 14(3) amended again in 2020 to slightly extend deadline; RIAS said amendment was for clarity and consistency
propositions.quote: Subsection 14(3) was amended again in 2020 with the effect of slightly extending the deadline. The RIAS for this amendment stated that it was for clarity and consistency.

paragraphs.summary: The court reviews RIAS showing subsection 14(3) amendments aimed at clarity and consistency, with no stated original purpose.

propositions.text: RIAS for original subsection 14(3) does not state its purpose, so RIAS overall may not help determine purpose
propositions.quote: Since the RIAS for the original version does not state the purpose of subsection 14(3), the RIAS’ as a whole may not provide much assistance in determining the purpose of the provision.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RIAS do not clarify subsection 14(3)'s purpose.

propositions.text: Text, context and purpose considerations may impact Decision and Tribunal may have reached different result if considered
propositions.quote: I conclude that these considerations concerning the text, context and purpose of subsection 14(3) may impact the Decision and that if they had been considered by the Tribunal, it may have reached a different result.

propositions.text: Decision is unreasonable as Tribunal failed to consider these considerations per Vavilov
propositions.quote: Accordingly, in accordance with the teaching in Vavilov, the Decision is unreasonable insofar as the Tribunal failed to take these considerations into account.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Decision is unreasonable for failing to consider subsection 14(3)'s text, context, and purpose, per Vavilov.

propositions.text: This finding suffices to dispose of judicial review; no need to consider other submissions
propositions.quote: This is sufficient to dispose of the judicial review application and it is not necessary to consider Prairie Pride’s other submissions.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds this issue sufficient to dispose of the judicial review without considering other submissions.

propositions.text: Allow application for judicial review with costs, set aside Tribunal decision, refer matter back for reconsideration
propositions.quote: I would allow the application for judicial review with costs, set aside the decision of the Tribunal, and refer the matter back to the Tribunal for reconsideration.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the judicial review, sets aside the Tribunal decision, and refers the matter back for reconsideration.
